job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Superintelligence. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Superintelligence (CAS) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the development of artificial superintelligence, meaning AI systems that vastly outperform humans across virtually all domains, poses a serious risk of human extinction, and that no one currently knows how to build such systems safely. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on the development of superintelligence, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I read the bill as a defense lawyer for a frontier lab would. Items are in section order, and my top priorities are at the end. The legal citations and the compute arithmetic are from memory and should be checked by counsel or policy staff.

## Section 2: Definitions

1. **§2(1)(A), "single training run."** The term is undefined, so developers can split work into sub-threshold runs, use staged pipelines, restart from checkpoints, or add large fine-tuning, RL, or distillation phases. The bill doesn't say whether compute spent on a base model counts toward a derivative model.

2. **§2(1)(A), fixed threshold.** The 10^26 figure has no update mechanism, no rulemaking authority, and no method for measuring or verifying compute. Algorithmic efficiency gains will make the threshold steadily less meaningful.

3. **§2(1)(A), compute as a proxy.** Compute is both over- and under-inclusive. Opponents can argue it bans ordinary frontier AI, since current frontier runs may already be near this level, while a highly capable low-compute system escapes (A) entirely. The word "superintelligence" appears only in the title and is never defined.

4. **§2(1)(A) vs. (B), "model" vs. "system."** Neither term is defined, and (A) says "model" while (B) says "system." A system built from several sub-threshold models, such as an agentic pipeline, falls outside (A). Consider borrowing the definition in 15 U.S.C. § 9401(3).

5. **§2(1)(A), runs in progress.** A model is covered once it was "trained using" more than 10^26 operations, so a run arguably isn't covered until it crosses the line. Nothing reaches runs that are planned or reasonably expected to exceed the threshold, and there is no attempt liability.

6. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** The Secretary is never identified. §6 refers to the Secretary of State, and Commerce is presumably intended.

7. **§2(1)(B), vague standard.** The phrases "substantially exceeding," "most," "cognitive tasks," and "human performance" (which humans?) have no benchmarks or criteria. Because criminal penalties attach, this invites vagueness and nondelegation challenges. It also sets a different, lower bar than the "vastly outperform" concept behind the title.

8. **§2(1)(B), no process.** The Secretary is not required to evaluate anything, and there are no notice procedures, timelines, evidentiary standards, or advisory-determination mechanism. A system can only be designated after it exists, so developers can't know in advance whether training is unlawful. That also undercuts proof of "willfulness" under §5(b), and a future administration could simply never use the authority.

9. **§2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and unincorporated associations ("corporation" may not cover them). It also omits lawful permanent residents and entities organized under federal, D.C., or territorial law ("State" is undefined). There is no ownership or control test, so a foreign-incorporated subsidiary of a U.S. company can train abroad unreached.

10. **§2(3), "advanced AI chip" and "data center."** Neither is defined, and there is no performance metric, so 50,000 older chips and 10,000 newer ones are treated alike. It's unclear whether chips are aggregated across sites, affiliates, or leased capacity, so operators can split clusters just under the threshold.

## Section 3: Prohibition

11. **§3(a), "train, develop, or deploy."** None of the verbs is defined. "Develop" could mean anything from research to writing code, and "deploy" doesn't clearly cover API access, internal use, open-weight release, hosting, or importing a foreign-built model.

12. **§3(a), reach.** The ban doesn't cover financing, supplying compute or chips, or knowingly assisting a prohibited project, and civil liability has no aiding-and-abetting hook. "Person in the United States" modifies the actor, so a foreign developer outside the U.S. serving U.S. users is arguably uncovered. "United States" is also undefined, and the bill is silent on jurisdiction and service of process over foreign defendants.

13. **§3(b), scope of grandfathering.** The exemption covers all of "train, develop, or deploy," so continued training, scaling up, fine-tuning, and arguably successor models derived from an existing system are exempt, with no capability ceiling. It also exempts a pre-enactment system that would qualify under (B), indefinitely.

14. **§3(b), "training began."** The term is undefined, so a token or placeholder run before enactment, or a new run initialized from an old checkpoint, could claim the exemption. The enactment-date cutoff also rewards rushing to start giant runs while the bill moves.

15. **§3(c), safety evaluation.** The exemption is undefined and purpose-based, with no limits on scale, no licensing, no oversight, no containment or security requirements, and no reporting. A company can self-label a training or deployment effort as "safety evaluation," which makes this probably the largest hole in the bill. As written it could even authorize training a covered system in order to evaluate it.

## Section 4: Registry

16. **§4(a), mechanics.** There is no registration deadline, no designated Commerce office, no required registration contents, and no rulemaking authority.

17. **§4(b), reporting content and timing.** "Describing the computing workloads" doesn't require model identity, FLOP totals, customers, or run duration. Quarterly reports can arrive months after a run is finished, and nothing requires advance notice of very large runs.

18. **§4, who reports.** Only facility operators report, and operators of cloud or colocation sites may not know what tenants are running. There is no know-your-customer duty, no tenant or developer disclosure obligation, and no registry of developers or training runs.

19. **§4 vs. §2(3), threshold mismatch.** On a rough back-of-envelope, about 10,000 H100-class chips at roughly 40% utilization could reach 10^26 FLOP in under a year. A facility well below 50,000 chips can therefore train a covered model without ever registering.

20. **§4, no teeth.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register or filing a false report carries no stated penalty. 18 U.S.C. § 1001 may partly backstop false certifications. There is also no audit, inspection, or subpoena authority and no whistleblower protection.

21. **§4, confidentiality.** The bill doesn't address trade-secret protection, FOIA treatment, or sharing data with DOJ or other agencies. That is both a likely industry objection and an enforcement gap.

## Section 5: Penalties

22. **§5(a), no enforcer or procedure.** The bill doesn't say who may bring a civil action or how. It also gives no injunctive authority, administrative process, state AG role, or private right of action.

23. **§5(a), cap too low.** At most $1,000,000 per day is about $365M per year, small against frontier-lab compute budgets. There is no minimum, no revenue scaling, and no inflation adjustment.

24. **§5(a), "each day on which the violation occurs."** It's unclear how continuing conduct such as a multi-month training run or ongoing deployment is counted. The default five-year limitations period (28 U.S.C. § 2462) would apply unless the bill says otherwise.

25. **§5, no remedies aimed at the model.** There is no authority to order a halt, delete or surrender weights, seize chips, forfeit assets, or disgorge profits. Fines alone can be treated as a cost of doing business.

26. **§5(b), "willfully."** This likely requires proof the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful, and arguably that the system was covered. Combined with the open-ended (B) definition, that is a high bar.

27. **§5(b), fine levels and liability.** "Fined under title 18" caps organizational fines at $500,000 per felony count unless prosecutors invoke the alternative fine of twice the gain or loss (18 U.S.C. § 3571(d)). There is no express responsible-corporate-officer or successor liability.

## Section 6: International Agreement

28. **§6, hortatory.** "Shall seek to negotiate" requires only effort, and it's unclear what must happen by the 18-month mark. "Equivalent" prohibitions are undefined, and there is no reporting to Congress, no mention of treaty ratification, no appropriations, and no consequence for failure.

29. **§6, no leverage or fallback.** The bill has no export-control, chip-supply, or import tools, so non-U.S. persons abroad are unconstrained if talks stall. That also feeds the "unilateral disarmament" objection.

## Section 7: Duration

30. **§7(b), sunset.** The sunset after 10 years applies regardless of any safety finding, so it overrides §7(a), and industry can simply wait it out. It effectively gives about 9.5 years of operative prohibition because of the §8 delay. If this came from the manager's amendment as a compromise, it directly conflicts with CAS's goals.

31. **§7(b), no saving clause.** Courts have sometimes held that prosecutions for violations of an expired temporary statute abate absent a saving clause. As written, unprosecuted violations and pending cases may be at risk when the Act lapses.

32. **§7(a), unlock standard.** "Can be developed safely" is undefined, and nothing obligates NASEM to produce a report, sets a timeline, or sets criteria. It's also unclear whether Congress may act without a report. One finding lifts the entire ban with no licensing or regulatory framework behind it, and the joint resolution is subject to presidential veto.

## Section 8 and Structural Issues

33. **§8 vs. §3(b) vs. §5(a), timing conflicts.** The prohibition starts 180 days after enactment, the grandfather cutoff is enactment, and the civil penalty applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment." Runs begun in the gap are lawful to train but unlawful to deploy afterward, and it's unclear whether they must stop on day 180. The penalty clause conflicts with the effective date, which creates fair-notice and ambiguity litigation risk.

34. **Whole bill, no severability clause.** If a court strikes (B), "develop," or another provision, the rest of the Act is exposed.

35. **Whole bill, no findings or jurisdictional hook.** There is no findings section on risk or interstate effects and no commerce element, which weakens the Commerce Clause defense for purely local development. Barring "develop" without narrowing language invites First Amendment challenges (courts have treated code as speech in some contexts).

36. **Whole bill, government activity.** The bill is silent on federal agencies, the military, intelligence, and national labs. The Dictionary Act's definition of "person" generally doesn't include the federal government, so government-run programs are likely uncovered, and contractors working for them are ambiguous.

## Suggested Priorities

- **Closes the ban in practice:** #15 (§3(c)), #13/#14 (§3(b)), #30/#31 (§7(b)), and #33 (timing gap).
- **Makes it unenforceable or fragile in court:** #7/#8 (§2(1)(B)), #22 (no enforcer), #26 (willfulness), and #34/#35 (severability and findings).
- **Lets companies route around it:** #1/#5 (compute definition), #9 (U.S. person), #12 (reach), and #18/#19 (registry coverage).

I can draft proposed amendment language for any of these, or a one-page version for Hill staff, if you'd like.
